4. Any determinate amount or quantity (as of length, time, heat, value) adopted as a standard of measurement for other amounts or quantities of the same kind.
5. (Math.)

Defn: A single thing, as a magnitude or number, regarded as an undivided whole. Abstract unit, the unit of numeration; one taken in the abstract; the number represented by 1. The term is used in distinction from concrete, or determinate, unit, that is, a unit in which the kind of thing is expressed; a unit of measure or value; as 1 foot, 1 dollar, 1 pound, and the like. — Complex unit (Theory of Numbers), an imaginary number of the form a + b-1, when a2 + b2 = 1. — Duodecimal unit, a unit in the scale of numbers increasing or decreasing by twelves. — Fractional unit, the unit of a fraction; the reciprocal of the denominator; thus, unit of the fraction — Integral unit, the unit of integral numbers, or 1. — Physical unit, a value or magnitude conventionally adopted as a unit or standard in physical measurements. The various physical units are usually based on given units of length, mass, and time, and on the density or other properties of some substance, for example, water. See Dyne, Erg, Farad, Ohm, Poundal, etc. — Unit deme (Biol.), a unit of the inferior order or orders of individuality. — Unit jar (Elec.), a small, insulated Leyden jar, placed between the electrical machine and a larger jar or battery, so as to announce, by its repeated discharges, the amount of electricity passed into the larger jar. — Unit of heat (Physics), a determinate quantity of heat adopted as a unit of measure; a thermal unit (see under Thermal). Water is the substance generally employed, the unit being one gram or one pound, and the temperature interval one degree of the Centigrade or Fahrenheit scale. When referred to the gram, it is called the gram degree. The British unit of heat, or thermal unit, used by engineers in England and in the United States, is the quantity of heat necessary to raise one pound of pure water at and near its temperature of greatest density (39.1º Fahr.) through one degree of the Fahrenheit scale. Rankine. — Unit of illumination, the light of a sperm candle burning 120 grains per hour. Standard gas, burning at the rate of five cubic feet per hour, must have an illuminating power equal to that of fourteen such candles. — Unit of measure (as of length, surface, volume, dry measure, liquid measure, money, weight, time, and the like), in general, a determinate quantity or magnitude of the kind designated, taken as a standard of comparison for others of the same kind, in assigning to them numerical values, as 1 foot, 1 yard, 1 mile, 1 square foot, 1 square yard, 1 cubic foot, 1 peck, 1 bushel, 1 gallon, 1 cent, 1 ounce, 1 pound, 1 hour, and the like; more specifically, the fundamental unit adopted in any system of weights, measures, or money, by which its several denominations are regulated, and which is itself defined by comparison with some known magnitude, either natural or empirical, as, in the United States, the dollar for money, the pound avoirdupois for weight, the yard for length, the gallon of 8.3389 pounds avoirdupois of water at 39.8º Fahr. (about 231 cubic inches) for liquid measure, etc.; in Great Britain, the pound sterling, the pound troy, the yard, or — Unit of power. (Mach.) See Horse power. — Unit of resistance. (Elec.) See Resistance, n., 4, and Ohm. — Unit of work (Physics), the amount of work done by a unit force acting through a unit distance, or the amount required to lift a unit weight through a unit distance against gravitation. See Erg, Foot Pound, Kilogrammeter. — Unit stress (Mech. Physics), stress per unit of area; intensity of stress. It is expressed in ounces, pounds, tons, etc., per square inch, square foot, or square yard, etc., or in atmospheres, or inches of mercury or water, or the like.
Defn: Capable of union by growth or otherwise. Owen.

lg.l: U`ni*ta"ri*an, n. Etym: [Cf. F. unitaire, unitairien, NL. unitarius.

div.p: 1. (Theol.)
Defn: One who denies the doctrine of the Trinity, believing that God exists only in one person; a unipersonalist; also, one of a denomination of Christians holding this belief.
2. One who rejects the principle of dualism.
3. A monotheist. [R.] Fleming.
Defn: Of or pertaining to Unitarians, or their doctrines.
Defn: The doctrines of Unitarians.
UNITARIANIZE U`ni*ta"ri*an*ize, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p Unitarianized; p. pr. & vb. n. Unitarianizing.]
Defn: To change or turn to Unitarian views.
1. Of or pertaining to a unit or units; relating to unity; as, the unitary method in arithmetic.

2. Of the nature of a unit; not divided; united. Unitary theory (Chem.), the modern theory that the molecules of all complete compounds are units, whose parts are bound together in definite structure, with mutual and reciprocal influence on each other, and are not mere aggregations of more or less complex groups; — distinguished from the dualistic theory.

lg.l: U*nite", v. t. [imp. & p. p. United; p. pr. & vb. n. Uniting.] Etym:
[L. unitus, p. p. of unire to unite, from unus one. See One.]

div.p: 1. To put together so as to make one; to join, as two or more constituents, to form a whole; to combine; to connect; to join; to cause to adhere; as, to unite bricks by mortar; to unite iron bars by welding; to unite two armies.

2. Hence, to join by a legal or moral bond, as families by marriage, nations by treaty, men by opinions; to join in interest, affection, fellowship, or the like; to cause to agree; to harmonize; to associate; to attach. Under his great vicegerent reign abide, United as one individual soul. Milton. The king proposed nothing more than to unite his kingdom in one form of worship. Clarendon.

lg.l: — To add; join; annex; attach. See Add.

div.p: 1. To become one; to be cemented or consolidated; to combine, as by adhesion or mixture; to coalesce; to grow together.
2. To join in an act; to concur; to act in concert; as, all parties united in signing the petition.

lg.l: U*nite", a Etym: [L. unitus, p. p. See Unite, v. t.]

div.p: Defn: United; joint; as, unite consent. [Obs.] J. Webster.

lg.l: Defn: Combined; joined; made one. United Brethren. (Eccl.) See
— United flowers (Bot.), flowers which have the stamens and pistils
— The United Kingdom, Great Britain and Ireland; — so named since
January 1, 1801, when the Legislative Union went into operation.
— United Greeks (Eccl.), those members of the Greek Church who
acknowledge the supremacy of the pope; — called also uniats.

div.p: Defn: In an united manner. Dryden.
Defn: One who, or that which, unites.
Defn: Not iterable; incapable of being repeated. [Obs.] "To play away an uniterable life." Sir T. Browne.

lg.l: U*ni"tion, n. Etym: [LL. unitio, from L. unire. See Unite,v. t.]
Defn: The act of uniting, or the state of being united; junction.
U"ni*tive, a. Etym: [LL. unitivus: cf. F. unitif.]

div.p: Defn: Having the power of uniting; causing, or tending to produce, union. Jer. Taylor.
Defn: In a unitive manner. Cudworth.

lg.l: U"nit*ize, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unitized; p. pr. & vb. n. Unitizing.]

div.p: Defn: To reduce to a unit, or one whole; to form into a unit; to unify.
Defn: Unity. [R.] H. Spenser.
UNITY U"ni*ty, n.; pl. Unities. Etym: [OE. unite, F. unité, L. unitas, from unus one. See One, and cf. Unit.]
1. The state of being one; oneness. Whatever we can consider as one thing suggests to the understanding the idea of unity. Locks.

Note: Unity is affirmed of a simple substance or indivisible monad, or of several particles or parts so intimately and closely united as to constitute a separate body or thing. See the Synonyms under Union.
2. Concord; harmony; conjunction; agreement; uniformity; as, a unity of proofs; unity of doctrine. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! Ps. cxxxiii. 1.
3. (Math.)

Defn: Any definite quantity, or aggregate of quantities or magnitudes taken as one, or for which 1 is made to stand in calculation; thus, in a table of natural sines, the radius of the circle is regarded as unity.
Note: The number 1, when it is not applied to any particular thing, is generally called unity.
4. (Poetry & Rhet.)

Defn: In dramatic composition, one of the principles by which a uniform tenor of story and propriety of representation are preserved; conformity in a composition to these; in oratory, discourse, etc., the due subordination and reference of every part to the development of the leading idea or the eastablishment of the main proposition.

Note: In the Greek drama, the three unities required were those of action, of time, and of place; that is, that there should be but one main plot; that the time supposed should not exceed twenty-four hours; and that the place of the action before the spectators should be one and the same throughout the piece.
5. (Fine Arts & Mus.)
Defn: Such a combination of parts as to constitute a whole, or a kind of symmetry of style and character.
6. (Law)
Defn: The peculiar characteristics of an estate held by several in joint tenancy.

Note: The properties of it are derived from its unity, which is fourfold; unity of interest, unity of title, unity of time, and unity of possession; in other words, joint tenants have one and the same interest, accruing by one and the same conveyance, commencing at the same time, and held by one and the same undivided possession. Unity of possession is also a joint possession of two rights in the same thing by several titles, as when a man, having a lease of land, afterward buys the fee simple, or, having an easement in the land of another, buys the servient estate.

lg.l: — Unity of type. (Biol.) See under Type.
— Union; oneness; junction; concord; harmony. See Union.

div.p: Defn: The quality or state of being univalent.

lg.l: U*niv"a*lent, a. Etym: [Uni- + L. valens, -entis, p. pr. See

div.p: Defn: Having a valence of one; capable of combining with, or of being substituted for, one atom of hydrogen; monovalent; — said of certain atoms and radicals.

lg.l: U"ni*valve, n. Etym: [Uni- + valve: cf. F. univalve.] (Zoöl.)

div.p: Defn: A shell consisting of one valve only; a mollusk whose shell is composed of a single piece, as the snails and conchs.

Note: Most univalves are spiral and are the shells of gastropods, but many belong to cephalopods and pteropods. A large number of univalves belonging to the gastropods are conical, cup-shaped, or shieldlike, as the limpets.

lg.l: U"ni*valve, U"ni*valved, a. Etym: [Cf. F. univalve.] (Bot. & Zoöl.)

div.p: Defn: Having one valve; as, a univalve shell or pericarp.
Defn: Same as Gastropoda.
Defn: Same as Univalve, a.
Defn: Having one degree of freedom or variability.
UNIVERSAL U`ni*ver"sal, a. Etym: Etym: [L. universalis: cf. F. universel, OF. also universal. See Universe.]

1. Of or pertaining to the universe; extending to, including, or affecting, the whole number, quantity, or space; unlimited; general; all-reaching; all-pervading; as, universal ruin; universal good; universal benevolence or benefice. "Anointed universal King." Milton. The universal cause Acts not by partial, but by general laws. Pope. This universal frame began. Dryden.
Note: Universal and its derivatives are used in common discourse for general and its derivatives. See General.

lg.l: 2. Constituting or considered as a whole; total; entire; whole; as,
At which the universal host up dent A shout that tore Hell's concave.

div.p: 3. (Mech.)
Defn: Adapted or adaptable to all or to various uses, shapes, sizes, etc.; as, a universal milling machine.
4. (Logic)

Defn: Forming the whole of a genus; relatively unlimited in extension; affirmed or denied of the whole of a subject; as, a universal proposition; — opposed to particular; e. g. (universal affirmative) All men are animals; (universal negative) No men are omniscient. Universal chuck (Mach.), a chuck, as for a lathe, having jaws which can be moved simultaneously so as to grasp objects of various sizes. — Universal church, the whole church of God in the world; the catholic church. See the Note under Catholic, a., 1. — Universal coupling. (Mach.) Same as Universal joint, below. — Universal dial, a dial by which the hour may be found in any part of the world, or under any elevation of the pole. — Universal instrument (Astron.), a species of altitude and azimuth instrument, the peculiarity of which is, that the object end of the telescope is placed at right angles to the eye end, with a prism of total reflection at the angle, and the eye end constitutes a portion of the horizontal axis of the instrument, having the eyepiece at the pivot and in the center of the altitude circle, so that the eye has convenient access to both at the same time. — Universal joint (Mach.), a contrivance used for joining two shafts or parts of a machine endwise, so that the one may give rotary motion to the other when forming an angle with it, or may move freely in all directions with respect to the other, as by means of a cross connecting the forked ends of the two shafts (Fig. 1). Since this joint can not act when the angle of the shafts is less than 140º, a double joint of the same kind is sometimes used for giving rotary motion at angles less than 140º (Fig. 2). — Universal umbel (Bot.), a primary or general umbel; the first or largest set of rays in a compound umbel; — opposed to partial umbel. A universal involucre is not unfrequently placed at the foot of a universal umbel.

lg.l: — General; all; whole; total. See General.

div.p: 1. The whole; the general system of the universe; the universe. [Obs.] Plato calleth God the cause and original, the nature and reason, of the universal. Sir W. Raleigh.

2. (Logic) (a) A general abstract conception, so called from being universally applicable to, or predicable of, each individual or species contained under it. (b) A universal proposition. See Universal, a., 4.
Defn: Of or pertaining to Universalism; Universalist. [R.]
Defn: The doctrine or belief that all men will be saved, or made happy, in the future state.
1. (Theol.)

lg.l: Defn: One who believes in Universalism; one of a denomination of

div.p: 2. One who affects to understand all the particulars in statements or propositions. [Obs.] Bentley.
Defn: Of or pertaining to Unversalists of their doctrines.
Defn: Of or pertaining to the whole; universal.
UNIVERSALITY U`ni*ver*sal"i*ty, n.; pl. Universalties. Etym: [Cf. F. universalité.]

Defn: The quality or state of being universal; unlimited extension or application; generality; — distinguished from particularity; as, the unversality of a proposition; the unversality of sin; the unversality of the Deluge.

lg.l: U`ni*ver"sal*ize, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Universalized; p. pr. & vb. n.

div.p: Defn: To make universal; to generalize. Coleridge.
Defn: In a universal manner; without exception; as, God's laws are universally binding on his creatures.
Defn: The quality or state of being universal; universality.
UNIVERSE U"ni*verse, n. Etym: [L. universum, from universus universal; unus one + vertere, versum, to turn, that is, turned into one, combined into one whole; cf. F. univers. See One, and Verse.]

Defn: All created things viewed as constituting one system or whole; the whole body of things, or of phenomena; the mundus of the Latins; the world; creation. How may I Adore thee, Author of this universe And all this good to man! Milton.

UNIVERSITY U`ni*ver"si*ty, n.; pl. Universities. Etym: [OE. universite, L. universitas all together, the whole, the universe, a number of persons associated into one body, a society, corporation, fr. universus all together, universal: cf. F. université. See Universe.]
1. The universe; the whole. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

2. An association, society, guild, or corporation, esp. one capable of having and acquiring property. [Obs.] The universities, or corporate bodies, at Rome were very numerous. There were corporations of bakers, farmers of the revenue, scribes, and others. Eng. Cyc.

3. An institution organized and incorporated for the purpose of imparting instruction, examining students, and otherwise promoting education in the higher branches of literature, science, art, etc., empowered to confer degrees in the several arts and faculties, as in theology, law, medicine, music, etc. A university may exist without having any college connected with it, or it may consist of but one college, or it may comprise an assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning. The present universities of Europe were, originally, the greater part of them, ecclesiastical corporations, instituted for the education of churchmen . . . What was taught in the greater part of those universities was suitable to the end of their institutions, either theology or something that was merely preparatory to theology. A. Smith.

Note: From the Roman words universitas, collegium, corpus, are derived the terms university, college, and corporation, of modern languages; and though these words have obtained modified significations in modern times, so as to indifferently applicable to the same things, they all agree in retaining the fundamental signification of the terms, whatever may have been added to them. There is now no university, college, or corporation, which is not a juristical person in the sense above explained [see def. 2, above]; wherever these words are applied to any association of persons not stamped with this mark, it is an abuse of terms. Eng. Cyc.
Defn: The extension of the advantages of university instruction by means of lectures and classes at various centers.
Defn: Of or pertaining to universology.
Defn: One who is versed in universology.
Defn: The science of the universe, and the relations which it involves.
Defn: The quality or state of being univocal. [R.] Sir T. Browne.
UNIVOCAL U*niv"o*cal, a. Etym: [L. univocus; unus one + vox, vocis, a voice, word. See One, and Voice.]
1. Having one meaning only; — contrasted with equivocal.
2. Having unison of sound, as the octave in music. See Unison, n., 2.
3. Having always the same drift or tenor; uniform; certain; regular. [R.] Sir T. Browne.
4. Unequivocal; indubitable. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.
1. (Aristotelian Logic)
Defn: A generic term, or a term applicable in the same sense to all the species it embraces.
2. A word having but one meaning.

lg.l: Defn: In a univocal manner; in one term; in one sense; not
How is sin univocally distinguished into venial and mortal, if the
venial be not sin Bp. Hall.

div.p: Defn: Agreement of name and meaning. [Obs.] Whiston.

lg.l: Un*join", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + join.]

div.p: Defn: To disjoin.

lg.l: Un*joint", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + joint.]

div.p: Defn: To disjoint.

lg.l: Un*joint"ed, a. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unjoint.]

div.p: 1. Disjointed; unconnected; hence, incoherent. Shak.
2. Etym: [Pref. un- + jointed.]
Defn: Having no joint or articulation; as, an unjointed stem.
1. Acting contrary to the standard of right; not animated or controlled by justice; false; dishonest; as, an unjust man or judge.
2. Contrary to justice and right; prompted by a spirit of injustice; wrongful; as, an unjust sentence; an unjust demand; an unjust accusation. — Un*just"ly, adv. — Un*just"ness, n.
Defn: Want of justice; injustice. [Obs.] Hales.
Defn: See Unked. [Prov. Eng.]
Defn: A European aquatic toad (Bombinator igneus). Its back is dark; its belly is marked with crimson. Called also feuerkröte.

lg.l: Un"ked, a. Etym: [Corrupted fr. uncouth, or OE. unkid; un- + p. p. of
AS. cyedhan to make known, fr. cuedh known. See Uncouth.]

div.p: 1. Odd; strange; ugly; old; uncouth. [Prov. Eng.]
2. Lonely; dreary; unkard. [Prov. Eng.] Weston is sadly unked without you. Cowper.
Defn: Unkempt. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*kempt", a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + kempt, p. p. of kemb.]

div.p: 1. Not combed; disheveled; as, an urchin with unkempt hair.
2. Fig.; Not smoothed; unpolished; rough. My rhymes be rugged and unkempt. Spenser.

lg.l: Un*ken"nel, v. t. Etym: [1st un- + kennel.]

div.p: 1. To drive from a kennel or hole; as, to unkennel a fox.
2. Fig.: To discover; to disclose. Shak.

lg.l: Un*kent", a. Etym: [Un- knot + ken to know.]

div.p: Defn: Unknown; strange. [Obs. or Scot.] W. Browne.
Defn: Uncouth. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]
Defn: Having no race or kindred; childless. [Obs. & R.] Shak.
1. Not kind; contrary to nature, or the law of kind or kindred; unnatural. [Obs.] "Such unkind abominations." Chaucer.

2. Wanting in kindness, sympathy, benevolence, gratitude, or the like; cruel; harsh; unjust; ungrateful. He is unkind that recompenseth not; but he is most unkind that forgetteth. Sir T. Elyot. — Un*kind"ly, adv. — Un*kind"ness, n.
Defn: Unkindness. Tennyson.
1. Not kindly; unkind; ungracious.
2. Unnatural; contrary to nature. [Obs.] "Unkindly crime." Spenser.
3. Unfavorable; annoying; malignant. Milton.

lg.l: Defn: Not kindred; not of the same kin. [Obs.] Rowe.
Un*king", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + king.]
Defn: To cause to cease to be a king. [R.]
Shall his condescension, therefore, unking him South.
Defn: The quality or condition of being unkinged; abolition of
Unkingship was proclaimed, and his majesty's statues thrown down.
Un*kiss", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + king.]
Defn: To cancel or annul what was done or sealed by a kiss; to cancel
Let me unkiss the oath 'twixt thee and me. Shak.

div.p: Defn: See Uncle. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*knight", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + knight.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of knighthood. Fuller.

lg.l: Un*knit", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + knit.]
Defn: To undo or unravel what is knitted together.
Fie, fie! unknit that threatening unkind brow. Shak.
Un*knot", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + knot.]

div.p: Defn: To free from knots; to untie.

lg.l: Un*know", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + know.]

div.p: 1. To cease to know; to lose the knowledge of. [Obs.]
2. To fail of knowing; to be ignorant of. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*know", a. Etym: [See Un- not, Know.]

div.p: Defn: Unknown. [Obs.] "French of Paris was to her unknow." Chaucer.

lg.l: For which bounty to us lent Of him unknowledged or unsent. B. Jonson.

div.p: 1. Not produced by labor or toil. "Unlabored harvests." Dryden.
2. Not cultivated; untitled; as, an unlabored field.
3. Not laboriously produced, or not evincing labor; as, an unlabored style or work. Tickell.

lg.l: Un*lace", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + lace.]

div.p: 1. To loose by undoing a lacing; as, to unlace a shoe.
2. To loose the dress of; to undress; hence, to expose; to disgrace. What's the matter, That you unlace your reputation thus Shak.
3. (Naut.)
Defn: To loose, and take off, as a bonnet from a sail, or to cast off, as any lacing in any part of the rigging of a vessel. Totten.

lg.l: Un*lade" v. t. Etym: [1st un- + lade.]

div.p: 1. To take the load from; to take out the cargo of; as, to unlade a ship or a wagon. The venturous merchant . . . Shall here unlade him and depart no more. Dryden.
2. To unload; to remove, or to have removed, as a load or a burden; to discharge. There the ship was to unlade her burden. Acts. xxi. 3.
1. Not laid or placed; not fixed. Hooker.
2. Not allayed; not pacified; not laid finally to rest. [R.] "Stubborn, unlaid ghost." Milton.
3. Not laid out, as a corpse. [R.] B. Jonson. Unlaid paper. See Laid paper, under Laid.

lg.l: Un*land", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + land.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of lands.

lg.l: Un*lap", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + lap.]

div.p: Defn: To unfold. [Obs.] Wyclif.

lg.l: Un*lash", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + lash.] (Naut.)

div.p: Defn: To loose, as that which is lashed or tied down.

lg.l: Un*latch", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Unlatched; p. pr. & vb. n.

div.p: Defn: To open or loose by lifting the latch; as, to unlatch a door.

lg.l: Un*laugh", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + laugh.]

div.p: Defn: To recall, as former laughter. [Obs. & R.] Sir T. More.

lg.l: Un*law", v. t. Etym: [1st un- + law.]

div.p: 1. To deprive of the authority or character of law. [Obs.]
2. To put beyond protection of law; to outlaw. [Obs.]
3. (Scots Law)
Defn: To impose a fine upon; to fine.
UNLAW Un*law", n. Etym: [Pref. un- + law.] (Scots Law) (a) Any transgression or offense against the law. (b) A fine imposed as a penalty for violation of the law.

lg.l: Un*lawed", a. Etym: [Pref. un- + lawed, p. p. of lawe.]

div.p: Defn: Not having the claws and balls of the forefeet cut off; — said of dogs.

lg.l: Defn: Not lawful; contrary to law.
— Un*law"ful*ness, n. Unlawful assembly. (Law) See under Assembly.

div.p: Defn: Not according to law; being or done in violation of law; unlawful. Milton.

lg.l: Un*lay", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + lay.] (Naut.)

div.p: Defn: To untwist; as, to unlay a rope.

lg.l: Un*learn", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + learn.]

div.p: 1. To forget, as what has been learned; to lose from memory; also, to learn the contrary of. I had learned nothing right; I had to unlearn everything. Milner.
2. To fail to learn. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
1. Not learned; untaught; uneducated; ignorant; illiterate.
2. Not gained by study; not known.

lg.l: 3. Not exhibiting learning; as, unlearned verses.
Un*leash", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + leash.]

div.p: Defn: To free from a leash, or as from a leash; to let go; to release; as, to unleash dogs.
Defn: Not leavened; containing no leaven; as, unleavened bread.
UNLESS Un*less", conj. Etym: [Formerly, onles, onlesse, onlesse that, that is, in less, in a less case. See On, and Less.]

Defn: Upon any less condition than (the fact or thing stated in the sentence or clause which follows); if not; supposing that not; if it be not; were it not that; except; as, we shall fail unless we are industrious.

lg.l: Note: By the omission of the verb in the dependent clause, unless was
frequently used prepositionally, — a construction common in
Here nothing breeds unless the nightly owl. Shak.

div.p: Defn: Not licked; hence, not properly formed; ungainly. Cf. To lick into shape, under Lick, v. Shak.
1. Not like; dissimilar; diverse; having no resemblance; as, the cases are unlike.

2. Not likely; improbable; unlikely. [Obsoles.] Unlike quantities (Math.), quantities expressed by letters which are different or of different powers, as a, b, c, a2, a3, xn, and the like. — Unlike signs (Math.), the signs plus (+) and minus (-).
Defn: Absence of likelihood.
Defn: The quality or state of being unlikely.
1. Not likely; improbable; not to be reasonably expected; as, an unlikely event; the thing you mention is very unlikely.
2. Not holding out a prospect of success; likely to fail; unpromising; as, unlikely means. Hooker.
3. Not such as to inspire liking; unattractive; disagreeable. [Obs.] "The unlikely eld of me." Chaucer.
Defn: In an unlikely manner.

lg.l: Un*lik"en, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + liken.]

div.p: Defn: To make unlike; to dissimilate. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Defn: The quality or state of being unlike; want of resemblance; dissimilarity. Tennyson.

lg.l: Un*lim"ber, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + limber.] (Mil.)

div.p: Defn: To detach the limber from; as, to unlimber a gun.
Defn: Illimitable. Locke.
1. Not limited; having no bounds; boundless; as, an unlimited expanse of ocean.
2. Undefined; indefinite; not bounded by proper exceptions; as, unlimited terms. "Nothing doth more prevail than unlimited generalities." Hooker.

3. Unconfined; not restrained; unrestricted. Ascribe not unto God such an unlimited exercise of mercy as may destroy his justice. Rogers. Unlimited problem (Math.), a problem which is capable of an infinite number of solutions. — Unlimited pump, a kind of deep-well pump placed at the level of the water, and operated from above ground. — Un*lim"it*ed*ly, adv. — Un*lim"it*ed*ness, n.

lg.l: Un*line", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + line.]

div.p: Defn: To take the lining out of; hence, to empty; as, to unline one's purse.

lg.l: Un*link", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + link.]

div.p: Defn: To separate or undo, as links; to uncoil; to unfasten. Shak.
Defn: Not liquidated; not exactly ascertained; not adjusted or settled. Unliquidated damages (Law), penalties or damages not ascertained in money. Burrill.
1. Not moistened or wet with liquor; dry. "Unliquored coach." Bp. Hall.
2. Not in liquor; not intoxicated; sober. Like an unliquored Silenus. Milton.
Defn: Not listed; specif. (New York Stock Exchange),
Defn: admitted to quotation in the unlisted department, that is, admitted to be dealt in on the floor, but not to the "regular list."

lg.l: Un*live", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + live.]

div.p: Defn: To [R.] Glanvill.

lg.l: Un*lived", a. Etym: [See 1st pref. Un-, and Life, Live.]

div.p: Defn: Bereft or deprived of life. [Obs.] Shak.

lg.l: Un*load", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + load.]

div.p: 1. To take the load from; to discharge of a load or cargo; to disburden; as, to unload a ship; to unload a beast.
2. Hence, to relieve from anything onerous.
3. To discharge or remove, as a load or a burden; as, to unload the cargo of a vessel.
4. To draw the charge from; as, to unload a gun.
5. To sell in large quantities, as stock; to get rid of. [Brokers' Cant, U. S.]
Defn: To perform the act of unloading anything; as, let unload now.
Defn: One who, or that which, unloads; a device for unloading, as hay from a wagon.
1. Not located or placed; not fixed in a place.
2. Not surveyed, or designated by marks, limits, or boundaries, as appropriated to some individual, company, or corporation; as, unlocated lands.

lg.l: Un*lock", v. t. Etym: [Cf. AS. unl. See 1st Un-, and Lock, v. t.]

div.p: 1. To unfasten, as what is locked; as, to unlock a door or a chest.
2. To open, in general; to lay open; to undo. Unlock your springs, and open all your shades. Pope. [Lord] unlock the spell of sin. J. H. Newman.

lg.l: Un*lodge", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + lodge.]

div.p: Defn: To dislodge; to deprive of lodgment. Carew.

lg.l: Un*look", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + look.]

div.p: Defn: To recall or retract, as a look. [R.] Richardson.

lg.l: Un*looked", a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + looked.]
Defn: Not observed or foreseen; unexpected; — generally with for.
She comes unlooked for, if she comes at all. Pope.

div.p: Defn: Not looked for; unexpected; as, an unlooked-for event.

lg.l: Un*loose", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- (intensive) + loose.]

div.p: Defn: To make loose; to loosen; to set free. Shak.
Defn: To become unfastened; to lose all connection or union.

lg.l: Un*loos"en, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- (intensive) + loosen.]

div.p: Defn: To loosen; to unloose.

lg.l: Un*lord", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + lord.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of the rank or position of a lord. Milton.
1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unlord.]
Defn: Deprived of the rank of a lord.
2. Etym: [Pref. un- + lorded.]
Defn: Not raised to the rank of a lord. Milton.

lg.l: Un*love", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + love.]

div.p: Defn: To cease to love; to hate. [Obs.]
Defn: Not lovely; not amiable; possessing qualities that excite dislike; disagreeable; displeasing; unpleasant. — Un*love"li*ness, n.
Defn: In an unlucky manner.
Defn: Quality or state of being unlucky.
1. Not lucky; not successful; unfortunate; ill-fated; unhappy; as, an unlucky man; an unlucky adventure; an unlucky throw of dice; an unlucky game.
Note: This word is properly applied to incidents in which failure results from chance or fortuity, as in games of hazard, rather than from lack or feebleness of effort.
2. Bringing bad luck; ill-omened; inauspicious. Haunt me not with that unlucky face. Dryden.
3. Mischievous; as, an unlucky wag. [Colloq.]

lg.l: Un*lute", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + lute.]

div.p: Defn: To separate, as things cemented or luted; to take the lute or the clay from. Boyle.
1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + made.]
Defn: Not yet made or formed; as, an unmade grave. Shak.
2. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unmake.]
Defn: Deprived of form, character, etc.; disunited.

lg.l: Un*mag"is*trate, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + magistrate.]
Defn: To divest of the office or authority of a magistrate. [Obs.]
Un*maid"en, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + maiden.]

div.p: Defn: To ravish; to deflower. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*make", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + make.]
Defn: To destroy the form and qualities of; to deprive of being; to
God does not make or unmake things to try experiments. T. Burnet.
Un*man", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + man.]

div.p: 1. To deprive of the distinctive qualities of a human being, as reason, or the like. [R.] South.
2. To emasculate; to deprive of virility.
3. To deprive of the courage and fortitude of a man; to break or subdue the manly spirit in; to cause to despond; to dishearten; to make womanish. Let's not unman each other. Byron.
4. To deprive of men; as, to unman a ship.

lg.l: Un*man"a*cle, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + manacle.]

div.p: Defn: To free from manacles. Tennyson.
Defn: Absence or lack of manhood. [Obs.] Chaucer.
1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unman.]
Defn: Deprived of manly qualities; deficient in vigor, strength, courage, etc.; weak; effeminate.
2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + man + -ed.] (Falconry)

lg.l: Defn: Not tamed; not made familiar with, or subject to, man; — also
Hood my unmanned blood bating in my cheeks With thy black mantle.

div.p: 3. Etym: [Pref. un- not + manned.]
Defn: Not furnished with men; as, an unmanned ship.

lg.l: Un*man"tle, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + mantle.]
Defn: To divest of a mantle; to uncover.
Nay, she said, but I will unmantle you. Sir W. Scott.
Un*mar"ry, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + marry.]

div.p: Defn: To annul the marriage of; to divorce. Milton.

lg.l: Un*mar"tyr, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + martyr.]

div.p: Defn: To degrade from the rank of a martyr. [Obs.] Fuller.

lg.l: Un*mas"cu*late, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + masculate.]

div.p: Defn: To emasculate. [Obs.] Fuller.

lg.l: Un*mask", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + mask.]

div.p: Defn: To strip of a mask or disguise; to lay open; to expose.
Defn: To put off a mask. Shak.
Defn: Incapable of being mastered or subdued. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Defn: Not material; immaterial. [Obs.] Daniel.
1. Having no meaning or signification; as, unmeaning words.
2. Not indicating intelligence or sense; senseless; expressionless; as, an unmeaning face. There pride sits blazoned on the unmeaning brow. Trumbull. — Un*mean"ing*ly, adv. — Un*mean"ing*ness, n.
Defn: Not meant or intended; unintentional. Dryden.

lg.l: Un*mech"an*ize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + mechanize.]

div.p: 1. To undo the mechanism of; to unmake; as, to unmechanize a structure. [Obs.] Sterne.
Defn: Not mechanized. Paley.

lg.l: Defn: Not meet or fit; not proper; unbecoming; unsuitable; — usually
followed by for. "Unmeet for a wife." Tennyson.
And all unmeet our carpet floors. Emerson.
Un*mem"ber, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + member.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of membership, as in a church.
Defn: The breeches; trousers. [Jocose]
Defn: Not merchantable; not fit for market; being of a kind, quality, or quantity that is unsalable. McElrath.

lg.l: Un*mer"cied, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + mercy.]

div.p: Defn: Unmerciful; merciless. [Obs.] Drayton.

lg.l: Defn: Not merciful; indisposed to mercy or grace; cruel; inhuman;

div.p: Defn: Utterly merciless. [Obs.] Joye.

lg.l: Un*mew", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + mew to confine.]

div.p: Defn: To release from confinement or restraint. Keats.

lg.l: Un*min"gle, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + mingle.]

div.p: Defn: To separate, as things mixed. Bacon.

lg.l: Defn: Incapable of being mistaken or misunderstood; clear; plain;
Un*mi"ter, Un*mi"tre, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + miter.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of a miter; to depose or degrade from the rank of a bishop. Milton.

lg.l: Un*mold", Un*mould", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + mold.]

div.p: Defn: To change the form of; to reduce from any form. "Unmolding reason's mintage." Milton.

lg.l: Defn: Destitute of money; not rich. [Written also unmonied.]
Un`mo*nop"o*lize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + monopolize.]
Defn: To recover or release from the state of being monopolized. [R.]
Unmonopolizing the rewards of learning and industry. Milton.

div.p: UNMOOR Un*moor", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + moor.] (Naut.) (a) To cause to ride with one anchor less than before, after having been moored by two or more anchors. (b) To loose from anchorage. See Moor, v. t.
Defn: To weigh anchor. Sir W. Scott.
Defn: Having no moral perception, quality, or relation; involving no idea of morality; — distinguished from both moral and immoral. — Un`mo*ral"i*ty, n.
Defn: Not restrained or tutored by morality. Norris.
Defn: Not arrayed in the dress of a morris dancer. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

lg.l: Un*mor"tise, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + mortise.]
Defn: To loosen, unfix, or separate, as things mortised together.
Defn: Not according to Moses; unlike Moses or his works.
By this reckoning Moses should be most un Mosaic. Milton.

div.p: Defn: Deprived of a mother; motherless.
Defn: Immovable. "Steadfast, unmovable." 1 Cor. xv. 58. Locke.
Defn: Immovably. [R.] J. Ellis.

lg.l: Defn: Not moved; fixed; firm; unshaken; calm; apathetic.
Un*muf"fle, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + muffle.]

div.p: 1. To take a covering from, as the face; to uncover.
2. To remove the muffling of, as a drum.
Defn: Immutable. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*muz"zle, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + muzzle.]

div.p: Defn: To loose from a muzzle; to remove a muzzle from.

lg.l: Un*nail", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + nail.]

div.p: Defn: To remove the nails from; to unfasten by removing nails.
Defn: Finished without a nap. I did not attempt her with a threadbare name, Unnapped with meritorious actions. Beau. & Fl.
Defn: Not natural; contrary, or not conforming, to the order of nature; being without natural traits; as, unnatural crimes.
Defn: To make unnatural. [R.] Hales.

lg.l: Un*na"ture, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + nature.]
Defn: To change the nature of; to invest with a different or contrary
A right heavenly nature, indeed, as if were unnaturing them, doth so
bridle them [the elements]. Sir P. Sidney.
Un*na"ture, n. Etym: [Pref. un- not + nature.]
Defn: The contrary of nature; that which is unnatural. [R.]
So as to be rather unnature, after all, than nature. H. Bushnell.
Defn: Not near; not close to; at a distance from. [Obs.] Davies
Defn: Not necessary; not required under the circumstances; unless;
needless; as, unnecessary labor, care, or rigor.

div.p: Defn: The state of being unnecessary; something unnecessary. [Obs.]
Defn: Being without neigbors. Cowper.

lg.l: Defn: Not neighborly; distant; reserved; solitary; exclusive.

div.p: Defn: Not in a neighborly manner. Shak.
Defn: Enervate. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*nerve", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + nerve.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of nerve, force, or strength; to weaken; to enfeeble; as, to unnerve the arm. Unequal match'd, . . . The unnerved father falls. Shak.

lg.l: Un*nest, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + nest.]

div.p: Defn: To eject from a nest; to unnestle. [R.] T. Adams.

lg.l: Un*nes"tle, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + nestle.]

div.p: Defn: Same as Unnest. [R.]
Defn: With difficulty. See Uneath. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Defn: Ignoble. Shak.
Defn: Ignobly. J. Fletcher.
Defn: Without nooks and corners; guileless. [Obs.] "Unnooked simplicity." Marston.

lg.l: Un*no"ti*fy, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + notify.]

div.p: Defn: To retract or withdraw a notice of. Walpole.
Defn: Not numbered; not counted or estimated; innumerable. Dryden.
Defn: Innumerable. [Obs.] "An unnumerable multitude." Udall.

lg.l: Un*nun", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + nun.]
Defn: To remove from condition of being a nun. [R.]
Many did quickly unnun and disfriar themselves. Fuller.

div.p: Defn: Disobedience. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Defn: Disobedient. [Obs.] Milton.
Defn: Want or neglect of observance; inobservance. Whitlock.

lg.l: Defn: Not obtrusive; not presuming; modest.

div.p: Defn: Inoffensive.
Defn: Not often. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*oil", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + oil.]

div.p: Defn: To remove the oil from. Dryden.
Defn: Producing no effect; inoperative. [Obs.] South.
Defn: Destitute of an operculum, or cover.

lg.l: Un*or"der, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + order.]

div.p: Defn: To countermand an order for. [R.]
Defn: Disorderly. [Obs.] Bp. Sanderson.
Defn: Disorderly; irregular; inordinate. [R.] — Un*or"di*nate*ly, adv. [R.]

Defn: Not organized; being without organic structure; specifically (Biol.), not having the different tissues and organs characteristic of living organisms, nor the power of growth and development; as, the unorganized ferments. See the Note under Ferment, n., 1.
1. Not originated; existing from all eternity. F. W. Newman.
2. Not yet caused to be, or to be made; as, possible inventions still unoriginated.
Defn: Without origin.
Defn: Destitute of a bony structure.
1. Ownerless. [Obs.] Shak.
2. Not owed; as, to pay money unowed.
UNOWNED Un*own"ed, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + (sense 1) owned possessed, and (sense 2) owned granted, acknowledged.]
1. Not owned; having no owner. Milton.
2. Not acknowledged; not avowed. Gay.

lg.l: Un*pack", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pack.]

div.p: 1. To separate and remove, as things packed; to open and remove the contents of; as, to unpack a trunk.
2. To relieve of a pack or burden. [R.] Shak.
Defn: One who unpacks.

lg.l: Un*pa"gan*ize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + paganize.]
Defn: To cause to cease to be pagan; to divest of pagan character.
Un*paint", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + paint.]

div.p: Defn: To remove the paint from; to efface, as a painting. Parnell.

lg.l: Defn: Not paired; not suited or matched.
And minds unpaired had better think alone. Crabbe.

div.p: Defn: Destitute of a palp.

lg.l: Un*pan"nel, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pannel.]

div.p: Defn: To take the saddle off; to unsaddle. [Obs.] Jervas.

lg.l: Un*par"a*dise, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + paradise.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of happiness like that of paradise; to render unhappy. [R.] Young.

lg.l: Defn: Having no paragon or equal; matchless; peerless. [R.]
Your unparagoned mistress is dead. Shak.

div.p: Defn: Having no parallel, or equal; unequaled; unmatched. The unparalleled perseverance of the armies of the United States, under every suffering and discouragement, was little short of a miracle. Washington.

lg.l: Un*parched", a. Etym: [Pref. un- not (intensive) parched.]
Defn: Dried up; withered by heat. [Obs.] "My tongue . . . unparched."

div.p: Defn: Not admitting of pardon or forgiveness; inexcusable.
Defn: Having no parent, or no acknowledged parent. [R.]

lg.l: Defn: Not parliamentary; contrary to the practice of parliamentary
Un*pas"tor, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pastor.]
Defn: To cause to be no longer pastor; to deprive of pastorship. [R.]

div.p: Defn: Not having a path. Shak.
Defn: Pathless. [R.] "The smooth, unpathwayed plain." Wordsworth.
Defn: Impatience. [Obs.]
Defn: Impatient. [Obs.] Wyclif.
1. Not paved; not furnished with a pavement. Hakewill.
2. Castrated. [Obs.] "Unpaved eunuch." Shak.

lg.l: Un*pay", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pay.]

div.p: Defn: To undo, take back, or annul, as a payment. Shak.
Defn: Absence or lack of peace. [Obs.] Testament of Love.
Defn: Not distinguished by a pedigree. [R.] Pollok.
1. Etym: [1st pref. un- (intensive) + peel.]
Defn: Thoroughly stripped; pillaged. [Obs.] Shak.
2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + peeled.]
Defn: Not peeled.
Defn: Incapable of having a peer, or equal.

lg.l: Defn: Having no peer; unequaled; unparalleled. "Unpeered excellence."
Un*peg", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + peg.]

div.p: Defn: To remove a peg or pegs from; to unfasten; to open. Shak.

lg.l: Un*pen", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pen.]

div.p: Defn: To release from a pen or from confinement. "If a man unpens another's water." Blackstone.
Defn: Impenetrable.
Defn: Impenitent. Sandys.

lg.l: Un*peo"ple, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + people.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of inhabitants; to depopulate. Shak.

lg.l: Un`per*e"gal, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + peregal.]

div.p: Defn: Unequal. [Obs.] Chaucer.

lg.l: Un*per"fect, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + perfect.]

div.p: Defn: To mar or destroy the perfection of. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.
Defn: Want of perfection; imperfection. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Defn: Imperishable.
Defn: Imperishably.

lg.l: Un`per*plex", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + perplex.]

div.p: Defn: To free from perplexity. [R.] Donne.

lg.l: Defn: The state of not being persuaded; disbelief; doubt. [R.] Abp.
Un`per*vert, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pervert.]

div.p: Defn: To free from perversion; to deliver from being perverted; to reconvert. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un`phi*los"o*phize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + philosophize.]

div.p: Defn: To degrade from the character of a philosopher. [R.] Pope.

lg.l: Un*pick, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- (intensive) + pick.]

div.p: Defn: To pick out; to undo by picking.

lg.l: Un*picked", a. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unpick.]

div.p: Defn: Picked out; picked open.
2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + picked.]
Defn: Not picked. Milton.

lg.l: Un*pin", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pin.]

div.p: Defn: To loose from pins; to remove the pins from; to unfasten; as, to unpin a frock; to unpin a frame.

lg.l: Un*pin"ion, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pinion.]
Defn: To loose from pinions or manacles; to free from restraint.

div.p: 1. Not pitied.
2. Pitiless; merciless. [Obs.] Shak.
1. Impious; wicked. [Obs.] "The life of the unpitous." Wyclif (Prov. xv. 8).
Defn: Impiety. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Defn: Want of piety. [Obs.]
Defn: Implacable. [Obs.]
Defn: Not placed.

lg.l: Un*plaid", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + plaid.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of a plaid.
Defn: Not deplored or bewailed; unlamented. [Obs.] Spenser.

lg.l: Un*plat", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + plat.]

div.p: Defn: To take out the folds or twists of, as something previously platted; to unfold; to unwreathe.
Defn: Not approving; disapproving. [Obs.] Shak.
1. Not used as a plea; not urged; as, an unpleaded excuse.
2. Not supported by pleas; undefended; as, an unpleaded suit.

lg.l: Defn: Not pleasant; not amiable or agreeable; displeasing; offensive.

div.p: 1. Want of pleasantry. [R.]
2. A state of disagreement; a falling out. Thackeray.
Defn: Unpleasant. [Obs.] "An unpleasive passion." Bp. Hall.

lg.l: Un*pleat", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pleat.]

div.p: Defn: To remove the plaits of; to smooth. W. Browne.

lg.l: Un*plight", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + plight.]

div.p: Defn: To unfold; to lay open; to explain. [Obs.] Chaucer.

lg.l: Un*plumb", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + plumb.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of lead, as of a leaden coffin. [R.] Burke.

lg.l: Un*plume", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + plume.]

div.p: Defn: To strip of plumes or feathers; hence, to humiliate.
1. Not poised or balanced.
2. Not poised or weighed; hence, regardless of consequences; unhesitating. [Obs.] Marston.

lg.l: Un*poi"son, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + poison.]

div.p: Defn: To remove or expel poison from. [Obs.] South.
1. Not having civil polity, or a regular form of government.
2. Impolitic; imprudent. [Obs.] Shak.

lg.l: Un*pol"ish, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + polish.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of polish; to make impolite.
Defn: Impolitic; imprudent.
Defn: Not polled. Specifically: (a) Not enumerated or registered; as, an unpolled vote or voter. (b) Not plundered. [Obs.] "Unpoll'd Arabian wealth." Fanshawe.

lg.l: Un*pope", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pope.]

div.p: 1. To divest of the character, office, or authority of a pope.
2. To deprive of a pope. [Obs.] Rome will never so far unpope herself as to part with her pretended supremacy. Fuller.
Defn: Importunate; troublesome with requests. [Obs.] Golden Boke.
Defn: Having no ports. [Obs.] "An unportuous coast." Burke.

lg.l: Un`pos*sess", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + possess.]

div.p: Defn: To be without, or to resign, possession of. [Obs.]
Defn: Impossibility. [R.] "Utter unpossibility." Poe.
Defn: Impossible. [R.]
Defn: Want of power; weakness. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.
Defn: Not powerful; weak. Cowley.
Defn: Impracticable; not feasible.

lg.l: Defn: Not practical; impractical. "Unpractical questions." H. James.
I like him none the less for being unpractical. Lowell.
Un*praise", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + praise.]

div.p: Defn: To withhold praise from; to deprive of praise. [R.]

lg.l: Un*pray, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pray.]

div.p: Defn: To revoke or annul by prayer, as something previously prayed for. [R.] Sir M. Hale.

lg.l: Defn: Not to be influenced or moved by prayers; obdurate. [R.]

div.p: Defn: Not prayed for. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

lg.l: Un*preach", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + preach.]

div.p: Defn: To undo or overthrow by preaching. [R.] De Foe.
Defn: Having no precedent or example; not preceded by a like case; not having the authority of prior example; novel; new; unexampled. — Un*prec"e*dent*ed*ly, adv.

lg.l: Un`pre*dict", v. i. Etym: [1st pref. un- + predict.]

div.p: Defn: To retract or falsify a previous prediction. Milton.
1. Not prejudiced; free from undue bias or prepossession; not preoccupied by opinion; impartial; as, an unprejudiced mind; an unprejudiced judge.

lg.l: 2. Not warped or biased by prejudice; as, an unprejudiced judgment.
Un*prel"a*ted, a. Etym: [1st pref. un- + prelate.]

div.p: Defn: Deposed from the office of prelate.
1. Not prevented or hindered; as, unprevented sorrows. Shak.
2. Not preceded by anything. [Obs.] Milton.
Defn: Not priced; being without a fixed or certain value; also, priceless. "Amethyst unpriced." Neale (Rhythm of St. Bernard).

lg.l: Un*priest", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + priest.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of priesthood; to unfrock. [R.] Milton.

lg.l: Un*prince", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + prince.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of the character or authority of a prince; to divest of principality of sovereignty. [R.] Swift.

lg.l: Un*prin"ci*ple, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + principle.]

div.p: Defn: To destroy the moral principles of. [R.]

lg.l: Un*prin"ci*pled, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + principled.]

div.p: Defn: Being without principles; especially, being without right moral principles; also, characterized by absence of principle. — Un*prin"ci*pled*ness, n.

lg.l: Un*pris"on, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + prison.]

div.p: Defn: To take or deliver from prison.
1. Not prized or valued; being without value. [Obs.]
2. Invaluable; being beyond estimation. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*prob"a*bly, adv. Etym: [Pref. un- not + probably.]

div.p: Defn: Improbably.
UNPROBABLY Un*prob"a*bly, adv. Etym: [Un- + L. probabilis approvable, fr. probare to approve. Cf. Probable.]
Defn: In a manner not to be approved of; improperly. [Obs. & R.] To diminish, by the authority of wise and knowing men, things unjustly and unprobably crept in. Strype.
Defn: Want of proficiency or improvement. Bp. Hall.
Defn: Want of profit; unprofitableness. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Defn: Profitless. [R.] Shak.

lg.l: Un*prom"ise, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + promise.]

div.p: Defn: To revoke or annul, as a promise. Chapman.

lg.l: Un*prop", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + prop.]

div.p: Defn: To remove a prop or props from; to deprive of support.

lg.l: Defn: Not proper or peculiar; improper. [Obs.] — Un*prop"er*ly, adv.
Un*pros"e*lyte, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + proselyte.]

div.p: Defn: To convert or recover from the state of a proselyte. Fuller.

lg.l: Un*prot"es*tant*ize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + protestantize.]
Defn: To render other than Protestant; to cause to change from
Protestantism to some other form of religion; to deprive of some
The attempt to unprotestantize the Church of England. Froude.
Un`pro*vide, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + provide.]
Defn: To deprive of necessary provision; to unfurnish.
Lest her . . . beauty unprovide my mind again. Shak.

div.p: Defn: Improvident. [Obs.] "Who for thyself art so unprovident.' Shak.
Defn: Imprudence. [Obs.]
Defn: Imprudent. [Obs.]

lg.l: Defn: Imprudent. [Obs.] "The most unwise and unprudential act."
Un*puck"er, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + pucker.]

div.p: Defn: To smooth away the puckers or wrinkles of.

lg.l: Un*pursed", a. Etym: [1st pref. un- + purse + -ed.]

div.p: 1. Robbed of a purse, or of money. [R.] Pollock.
2. Taken from the purse; expended. [Obs.] Gower.

lg.l: Un*qual"i*fy, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + quality.]

div.p: Defn: To disqualify; to unfit. Swift.

lg.l: Un*qual"i*tied, a. Etym: [1st pref. un- + quality.]

div.p: Defn: Deprived of the usual faculties. [Obs.] Shak.

lg.l: Un*queen", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + queen.]

div.p: Defn: To divest of the rank or authority of queen. Shak.
1. Not questionable; as, an unquestionable title.

lg.l: 2. Not inviting questions or conversation. [R.] Shak.

div.p: 1. Not called in question; not doubted.
2. Not interrogated; having no questions asked; not examined or examined into. Shak. She muttering prayers, as holy rites she meant, Through the divided crowd unquestioned went. Dryden.
3. Indisputable; not to be opposed or impugned. Their unquestioned pleasures must be served. B. Jonson.
Defn: Not quick. [R.] Daniel.

lg.l: Un*qui"et, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + quiet.]

div.p: Defn: To disquiet. [Obs.] Ld. Herbert.

lg.l: Defn: Not quiet; restless; uneasy; agitated; disturbed.

div.p: Defn: Uneasiness; inquietude.

lg.l: Un*rav"el, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- (intensive) + ravel.]

div.p: 1. To disentangle; to disengage or separate the threads of; as, to unravel a stocking.
2. Hence, to clear from complication or difficulty; to unfold; to solve; as, to unravel a plot.
3. To separate the connected or united parts of; to throw into disorder; to confuse. "Art shall be conjured for it, and nature all unraveled." Dryden.
Defn: To become unraveled, in any sense.
Defn: The act of unraveling, or the state of being unraveled.
Defn: Not shaven. [R.] Milton.
1. Not read or perused; as, an unread book. Hooker.
2. Not versed in literature; illiterate. Dryden.
Defn: The quality or state of being unready.
1. Not ready or prepared; not prompt; slow; awkward; clumsy. Dryden. Nor need the unready virgin strike her breast. Keble.
2. Not dressed; undressed. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*read"y, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + ready.]

div.p: Defn: To undress. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.
Defn: Not real; unsubstantial; fanciful; ideal.
Defn: The quality or state of being unreal; want of reality.

lg.l: Un*re"al*ize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + realize.]
Defn: To make unreal; to idealize.
His fancy . . . unrealizes everything at a touch. Lowell.

div.p: Defn: In an unreal manner; ideally.

lg.l: Un*rea"son, n. Etym: [Pref. un- not + reason.]
Defn: Want of reason; unreasonableness; absurdity. Abbot of Unreason.
See Abbot of Misrule, under Abbot.
Un*rea"son, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + reason.]
Defn: To undo, disprove, or refute by reasoning. [Obs.]
To unreason the equity of God's proceedings. South.
Defn: Not reasonable; irrational; immoderate; exorbitant.
Defn: Not supported by reason; unreasonable. "Unreasoned habits."

div.p: Defn: To unwind; to disentangle; to loose. [Obs.] Spenser.

lg.l: Un*reaved", a. Etym: [See Un- not, and, for -reaved, cf. Rive, and
Defn: Not torn, split, or parted; not torn to pieces. [Obs.] Bp.

div.p: Defn: Not deserving rebuke or censure; blameless. 1 Tim. vi. 14.
Defn: Incurable. [Obs.] "Some unrecuring wound." Shak.
Defn: Not redeemed.

lg.l: Un*reeve", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + reeve, v. t.] (Naut.)

div.p: Defn: To withdraw, or take out, as a rope from a block, thimble, or the like.

lg.l: Defn: Want of reformation; state of being unreformed. [Obs.] Bp.

div.p: Defn: The quality or state of being unregenerate. Glanvill.
Defn: Not regenerated; not renewed in heart; remaining or being at enmity with God.
Defn: Unregeneracy.

lg.l: Un*rein", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + rein.]

div.p: Defn: To loosen the reins of; to remove restraint from. Addison.

lg.l: Defn: Not relenting; unyielding; rigid; hard; stern; cruel.

div.p: Defn: Not reliable; untrustworthy. See Reliable. — Un`re*li"a*ble*ness, n. Alcibiades . . . was too unsteady, and (according to Mr. Coleridge's coinage) "unreliable;" or perhaps, in more correct English, too "unrelyuponable." De Quincey.
Defn: Irreligious. Wordsworth.
Defn: Want of remembrance; forgetfulness. I. Watts.

lg.l: Defn: Not remitting; incessant; continued; persevering; as,
Un`re*morse"less, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not (intensive) + remorseless.]

div.p: Defn: Utterly remorseless. [Obs. & R.] "Unremorseless death." Cowley.
Defn: Impenitence. [R.]
Defn: Not capable of being reprieved. Shak.
Defn: Not liable to be reproached; irreproachable.
1. Not reproved. Sandys.
2. Not having incurred reproof, blameless. [Obs.] In unreproved pleasures free. Milton.
Defn: Disreputable.

lg.l: Defn: Absence of reverse; frankness; freedom of communication. T.
Defn: Not reserved; not kept back; not withheld in part;

div.p: Defn: Nonresistance; passive submission; irresistance. Bp. Hall.
1. Not resisted; unopposed. Bentley.
2. Resistless; as, unresisted fate. [R.] Pope.
Defn: Irresistible. W. Temple.
Defn: Disrespect. [Obs.] "Unrespect of her toil." Bp. Hall.

lg.l: Defn: Want of rest or repose; unquietness; sleeplessness; uneasiness;
Is this, quoth she, the cause of your unrest! Chaucer.
Can calm despair and wild unrest Be tenants of a single breast

div.p: Defn: Freedom from restraint; freedom; liberty; license.

lg.l: Defn: Causing unrest; disquieting; as, unresty sorrows. [Obs.]

div.p: Defn: Not furnished with a revenue. [R.] Milton.
Defn: Absence or lack of reverence; irreverence. [Obs.] Wyclif.
1. Not reverend.
2. Disrespectful; irreverent. [Obs.] Shak.
Defn: Irreverent. [R.] Shak.
Defn: Irreverently. [R.] B. Jonson.

lg.l: Un*rid"dle, v. t. & i. Etym: [1st pref. un- + riddle.]

div.p: Defn: To read the riddle of; to solve or explain; as, to unriddle an enigma or a mystery. Macaulay. And where you can't unriddle, learn to trust. Parnell.
Defn: One who unriddles. Lovelace.

lg.l: Un*rig", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + rig.] (Naut.)

div.p: Defn: To strip of rigging; as, to unrig a ship. Totten.

lg.l: Un*right", a. Etym: [AS. unriht. See Un- not, and Right.]

div.p: Defn: Not right; wrong. [Obs.] Gower.

lg.l: Nor did I you never unright. Chaucer.
Un*right", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + right.]

div.p: Defn: To cause (something right) to become wrong. [Obs.] Gower.
UNRIGHTEOUS Un*right"eous, a. Etym: [OE. unrightwise, AS. unrihtwis. See Un- not, and Righteous.]
1. Not righteous; evil; wicked; sinful; as, an unrighteous man.

lg.l: 2. Contrary to law and equity; unjust; as, an unrighteous decree or

div.p: Defn: Not having a ring, as in the nose. "Pigs unringed." Hudibras.

lg.l: Defn: Free from rioting. [Obs.] "A chaste, unrioted house." May
Un*rip", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- (intensive) + rip.]

div.p: Defn: To rip; to cut open. Bacon.
1. Not ripe; as, unripe fruit.
2. Developing too early; premature. Sir P. Sidney.
Defn: Quality or state of being unripe.
Defn: Having no rival; without a competitor; peerless. [Spelt also unrivalled.] Pope.

lg.l: Un*riv"et, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + rivet.]

div.p: Defn: To take out, or loose, the rivets of; as, to unrivet boiler plates.

lg.l: Un*robe", v. t. & i. Etym: [1st pref. un- + robe.]

div.p: Defn: To disrobe; to undress; to take off the robes.

lg.l: Un*roll", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + roll.] [Written also unrol.]

div.p: 1. To open, as what is rolled or convolved; as, to unroll cloth; to unroll a banner.
2. To display; to reveal. Dryden.
3. To remove from a roll or register, as a name. If I make not this cheat bring out another . . . let me be unrolled and my name put in the book of virtue! Shak.
1. Not subjected to Roman arms or customs. J. Whitaker.
2. (Eccl.)

lg.l: Defn: Not subjected to the principles or usages of the Roman Catholic
Un*roof", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + roof.]

div.p: Defn: To strip off the roof or covering of, as a house. Shak.
1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unroof.]
Defn: Stripped of a roof, or similar covering. Broken carriages, dead horses, unroofed cottages, all indicated the movements. Sir W. Scott.
2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + roofed.]
Defn: Not yet roofed.

lg.l: Un*roost", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + roost.]

div.p: Defn: To drive from the roost. Shak.

lg.l: Un*root", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + root.]

div.p: Defn: To tear up by the roots; to eradicate; to uproot.
Defn: To be torn up by the roots. Beau. & Fl.

lg.l: Un*rude", a. Etym: [Pref. un- + rude. In sense 2 un- is intensive.]

div.p: 1. Not rude; polished. Herrick.
2. Excessively rude. [Obs. & R.] "See how the unrude rascal backbites him." B. Jonson.

lg.l: Un*ruf"fle, v. i. Etym: [1st pref. un- + ruffle.]

div.p: Defn: To cease from being ruffled or agitated. Dryden.

lg.l: Un*ruf"fled, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + ruffled.]
Defn: Not ruffled or agitated; smooth; calm; tranquil; quiet.
Calm and unruffled as a summer's sea. Addison.

div.p: Defn: Not ruined or destroyed. [Obs.] "Unruinated towers." Bp. Hall.
1. Not governed or controlled. "Unruled and undirected." Spenser.
2. Not ruled or marked with lines; as, unruled paper.

lg.l: Defn: Unruliness. [Obs.] "Breaking forth with rude unruliment."

div.p: Defn: Quality or state unruly.
UNRULY Un*rul"y, a. [Compar. Unrulier (, superl. Unruliest.] Etym: [Pref. un- not + rule. Cf. Ruly.]

Defn: Not submissive to rule; disregarding restraint; disposed to violate; turbulent; ungovernable; refractory; as, an unruly boy; unruly boy; unruly conduct. But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. James iii. 8.

lg.l: Un*rum"ple, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + rumple.]

div.p: Defn: To free from rumples; to spread or lay even,

lg.l: Un*sac"ra*ment, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sacrament.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of sacramental character or efficacy; as, to unsacrament the rite of baptism. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*sad", a. Etym: [AS. unsæd unsated, insatiable. See Un- not, and
O, stormy people, unsad and ever untrue. Chaucer.
Un*sad"den, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sadden.]

div.p: Defn: To relieve from sadness; to cheer. [R.] Whitlock.

lg.l: Un*sad"dle, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + saddle.]

div.p: 1. To strip of a saddle; to take the saddle from, as a horse.
2. To throw from the saddle; to unhorse.
Defn: Infirmity; weakness. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Defn: The quality or state of being in peril; absence of safety; insecurity. Bacon.

lg.l: Un*saint", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + saint.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of saintship; to deny sanctity to. [R.] South.
Defn: Unbecoming to a saint. Gauden.
Defn: That which can not be sold. Byron.
Defn: Absence or lack of sanctification. Shak.
Defn: Quality of being unsatiable; insatiability. [Obs.]
Defn: Insatiate. Dr. H. More.
Defn: Dissatisfaction. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
1. Capable of absorbing or dissolving to a greater degree; as, an unsaturated solution.
2. (Chem.)
Defn: Capable of taking up, or of uniting with, certain other elements or compounds, without the elimination of any side product; thus, aldehyde, ethylene, and ammonia are unsaturated.
Defn: The quality or state of being unsaturated.

lg.l: Un*say, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + say.]

div.p: Defn: To recant or recall, as what has been said; to refract; to take back again; to make as if not said. You can say and unsay things at pleasure. Goldsmith.

lg.l: Un*scale", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + scale.]

div.p: Defn: To divest of scales; to remove scales from. [An eagle] purging and unscaling her long-abused sight at the fountain itself of heavenly radiance. Milton.
Defn: Not be escaped; inevitable. [Obs.] Wyclif.
1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + sceptered.]
Defn: Having no scepter.
2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + scepter.]
Defn: Deprived of a scepter.
Defn: Want of science or knowledge; ignorance. [Obs.] If that any wight ween a thing to be otherwise than it is, it is not only unscience, but it is deceivable opinion. Chaucer.

lg.l: Un*screw", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + screw.]

div.p: Defn: To draw the screws from; to loose from screws; to loosen or withdraw (anything, as a screw) by turning it.
Defn: Inscrutable. [R.]
Defn: Destitute of an escutcheon. [R.] Pollock.

lg.l: Un*seal", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + seal.]
1. To break or remove the seal of; to open, as what is sealed; as, to
Unable to unseal his lips beyond the width of a quarter of an inch.

div.p: 2. To disclose, as a secret. [Obs.] The Coronation.

lg.l: Un*seam, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + seam.]
Defn: To open the seam or seams of; to rip; to cut; to cut open.
Defn: Not searchable; inscrutable; hidden; mysterious.
The counsels of God are to us unsearchable. Rogers.
Un*sea"son, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + season.]

div.p: 1. To make unseasoned; to deprive of seasoning.
2. To strike unseasonably; to affect disagreeably or unfavorably. [Obs.] Why do I send this rustic madrigal, That may thy tuneful ear unseason quite Spenser.

Defn: Not seasonable; being, done, or occurring out of the proper season; ill-timed; untimely; too early or too late; as, he called at an unseasonable hour; unseasonable advice; unseasonable frosts; unseasonable food. — Un*sea"son*a*ble*ness, n. — Un*sea"son*a*bly, adv.
1. Not seasoned.
2. Untimely; ill-timed. [Obs.] Shak.

lg.l: Un*seat", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + seat.]

div.p: 1. To throw from one's seat; to deprive of a seat. Cowper.
2. Specifically, to deprive of the right to sit in a legislative body, as for fraud in election. Macaulay.
1. Not seconded; not supported, aided, or assisted; as, the motion was unseconded; the attempt was unseconded.
2. Not exemplified a second time. [Obs.] "Strange and unseconded shapes of worms." Sir T. Browne.

lg.l: Un*se"cret, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + secret.]

div.p: Defn: To disclose; to divulge. [Obs.] Bacon.

lg.l: Un*se"cret, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + secret.]

div.p: Defn: Not secret; not close; not trusty; indiscreet. [Obs.] "We are unsecret to ourselves." Shak.

lg.l: Un*sec"u*lar*ize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + secularize.]

div.p: Defn: To cause to become not secular; to detach from secular things; to alienate from the world.
Defn: Insecure. [R.] Milton.

lg.l: Un*seel", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + seel.]

div.p: Defn: To open, as the eyes of a hawk that have been seeled; hence, to give light to; to enlighten. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

lg.l: Un*seem", v. i. Etym: [1st pref. un- + seem.]

div.p: Defn: Not to seem. [Obs.] Shak.
Defn: Unbeseeming; not fit or becoming.
Defn: The quality or state of being unseemly; unbecomingness. Udall.

lg.l: An unseemly outbreak of temper. Hawthorne.

div.p: Defn: In an unseemly manner.
1. Not seen or discovered.
2. Unskilled; inexperienced. [Obs.] Clarendon.
Defn: Not seldom; frequently. [R.]

lg.l: Un*se"ly, a. Etym: [AS. uns. See Un- not, and Silly.]

div.p: Defn: Not blessed or happy; wretched; unfortunate. [Written also unsilly.] [Obs.] Chaucer. — Un*se"li*ness, n. [Obs.] Chaucer.

lg.l: Un*sem"i*nared, a. Etym: [See 1st Un-, and Semen.]

div.p: Defn: Deprived of virility, or seminal energy; made a eunuch. [Obs.]

lg.l: Defn: Wanting a distinct meaning; having no certain signification.

div.p: Defn: Insensible. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*sen"su*al*ize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sensualize.]

div.p: Defn: To elevate from the domain of the senses; to purify. Coleridge.
Defn: Inseparable. [Obs.] "In love unseparable." Shak.
Defn: Neglect of duty; idleness; indolence. [Obs.] Massinger.
Defn: Not set; not fixed or appointed.

lg.l: Un*set"tle, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + settle.]

div.p: Defn: To move or loosen from a settled position or state; to unfix; to displace; to disorder; to confuse.
Defn: To become unsettled or unfixed; to be disordered. Shak.
Defn: The quality or state of being unsettled.
Defn: The act of unsettling, or state of being unsettled; disturbance. J. H. Newman.

lg.l: Un*sev"en, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + seven.]
Defn: To render other than seven; to make to be no longer seven.
[Obs. & R.] "To unseven the sacraments of the church of Rome."
Un*sew", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sew.]

div.p: Defn: To undo, as something sewn, or something inclosed by sewing; to rip apart; to take out the stitches of.

lg.l: Un*sex", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Unsexed; p. pr. & vb. n. Unsexing.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of sex, or of qualities becoming to one's sex; esp., to make unfeminine in character, manners, duties, or the like; as, to unsex a woman.

lg.l: Defn: Not sexual; not proper or peculiar to one of the sexes. De
Un*shac"kle, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shackle.]

div.p: Defn: To loose from shackles or bonds; to set free from restraint; to unfetter. Addison.
Defn: Not capable of being shaken; firm; fixed. Shak. J. S. Mill.
Defn: Unshaken. [Obs.] Shak.

lg.l: Un*shale", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shale.]
Defn: To strip the shale, or husk, from; to uncover. [Obs.]
I will not unshale the jest before it be ripe. Marston.
Un*shape, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shape.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of shape, or of proper shape; to disorder; to confound; to derange. [R.] Shak.

lg.l: Un*shaped", Un*shap"en, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + shaped, shapen.]

div.p: Defn: Not shaped; shapeless; misshapen; deformed; ugly.

lg.l: Un*sheathe", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sheath.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of a sheath; to draw from the sheath or scabbard, as a sword. To unsheathe the sword, to make war.
1. Not parted or divided, as the hair. [Obs.] Spenser.
2. Not spilt, or made to flow, as blood or tears. Milton.

lg.l: Un*shell", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shell.]

div.p: Defn: To strip the shell from; to take out of the shell; to hatch.

lg.l: Un*shelve", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shelve.]

div.p: Defn: To remove from, or as from, a shelf.
Defn: Not shent; not disgraced; blameless. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

lg.l: Un*sher"iff, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sheriff.]

div.p: Defn: To depose from the office of sheriff. [R.]
Defn: To unshut. [Obs.] Chaucer.
1. That may
2. Shiftless; helpless. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*ship", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + ship.]

div.p: 1. To take out of a ship or vessel; as, to unship goods.
2. (Naut.)
Defn: To remove or detach, as any part or implement, from its proper position or connection when in use; as, to unship an oar; to unship capstan bars; to unship the tiller.
Defn: The act of unshipping, or the state of being unshipped; displacement.

lg.l: Un*shot", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shot.]

div.p: Defn: To remove the shot from, as from a shotted gun; to unload.
Defn: Not hit by a shot; also, not discharged or fired off.

lg.l: Un*shout", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shout.]

div.p: Defn: To recall what is done by shouting. [Obs.] Shak.

lg.l: Un*shroud" (, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shroud.]

div.p: Defn: To remove the shroud from; to uncover. P. Fletcher.
Defn: Being without shrubs.

lg.l: Un*shut", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shut.]

div.p: Defn: To open, or throw open. [Obs.] Chaucer.

lg.l: Un*shut"ter, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + shutter.]

div.p: Defn: To open or remove the shutters of. T. Hughes.

Defn: Doing or done without sight; not seeing or examining. [Colloq.] Unsight unseen, a colloquial phrase, denoting unseeing unseen, or unseen repeated; as, to buy a thing unsight unseen, that is, without seeing it. For to subscribe, unsight, unseen, To a new church discipline. Hudibras. There was a great confluence of chapmen, that resorted from every part, with a design to purchase, which they were to do "unsight unseen." Spectator.
Defn: Invisible. [Obs.]
1. Not sighted, or seen. Suckling.
Defn: Not aimed by means of a sight; also, not furnished with a sight, or with a properly adjusted sight; as, to shoot and unsighted rife or cannon.
Defn: Insignificant. [Obs.] Holland.
Defn: See Unsely. [Obs.]
Defn: Absence of simplicity; artfulness. C. Kingsley.

lg.l: Un*sin", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sin.]
Defn: To deprive of sinfulness, as a sin; to make sinless. [Obs.]
Defn: Not sincere or pure; insincere. [Obs.] Dryden.
Defn: The quality or state of being unsincere or impure; insincerity.
Un*sin"ew, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sinew.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of sinews or of strength. [R.] Dryden.

lg.l: Un*sis"ter, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sister.]

div.p: Defn: To separate, as sisters; to disjoin. [Poetic & R.] Tennyson.
Defn: Not sisterly. Richardson.
Defn: Unresisting. [Obs.] "The unsisting postern." Shak.

lg.l: Defn: Not sitting well; unbecoming. [Obs.] "Unsitting words." Sir T.

div.p: Defn: Want of skill; ignorance; unskillfulness. [Obs.] Sylvester.
1. Not skillful; inexperienced; awkward; bungling; as, an unskillful surgeon or mechanic; an unskillful logician.

lg.l: Though it make the unskillful laugh, can not but make the judicious

div.p: Defn: Not slacked; unslaked; as, unslacked lime.
Defn: Not slaked; unslacked; as, an unslaked thirst; unslaked lime.

lg.l: Un*sling", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sling.] (Naut.)

div.p: Defn: To take off the slings of, as a yard, a cask, or the like; to release from the slings. Totten.

lg.l: Un*sluice", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sluice.]

div.p: Defn: To sluice; to open the sluice or sluices of; to let flow; to discharge. Dryden.
Defn: The quality or state of being unsociable; unsociableness.

lg.l: Defn: Not sociable; not inclined to society; averse to companionship
or conversation; solitary; reserved; as, an unsociable person or
Un*sock"et, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + socket.]

div.p: Defn: To loose or take from a socket.
Defn: Not soft; hard; coarse; rough. [Obs.] "Bristles of his beard unsoft." Chaucer.

lg.l: Un*soft", adv. Etym: [AS. uns. See Un- not, and Soft.]
Un*sol"der, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + solder.]

div.p: Defn: To separate or disunite, as what has been soldered; hence, to divide; to sunder. [Formerly written also unsoder.] Tennyson.
Defn: Not equipped like a soldier; unsoldierlike. [Obs.] J. Fletcher.

lg.l: Un*sol"em*nize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + solemnize.]

div.p: Defn: To divest of solemnity.
UNSONABLE Un*so"na*ble, a. Etym: [Pref. un- + L. sonabilis sounding, from sonare to sound.]
Defn: Incapable of being sounded. [Obs.]

lg.l: Un*son"sy, a. Etym: [See Un- not, and Soncy.]

div.p: Defn: Not soncy (sonsy); not fortunate. [Scot.]

lg.l: Un*soot", a. Etym: [AS. unsw. See Un- not, and Sweet.]

div.p: Defn: Not sweet. [Obs.] Spenser.

lg.l: Defn: Not sophisticated; pure; innocent; genuine.

div.p: Defn: Not sorrowed for; unlamented. Beau. & Fl.
1. Not sorted; not classified; as, a lot of unsorted goods.
2. Not well selected; ill-chosen. The purpose you undertake is dangerous; the friends you named uncertain; the time itself unsorted. Shak.

lg.l: Un*soul", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + soul.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of soul, spirit, or principle. [R.] Shelton.

lg.l: Defn: Not sound; not whole; not solid; defective; infirm; diseased.
Un*spar", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + spar.]

div.p: Defn: To take the spars, stakes, or bars from. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

lg.l: Un*spar"ing, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + sparing, p. pr. of spare.]

div.p: 1. Not sparing; not parsimonious; liberal; profuse. Burke.

lg.l: Un*speak", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + speak.]
Defn: To retract, as what has been spoken; to recant; to unsay. [R.]
Un*speak"a*ble, a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + speakable.]
Defn: Not speakable; incapable of being uttered or adequately
described; inexpressible; unutterable; ineffable; as, unspeakable
Ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. 1 Pet. i. 8.

div.p: Defn: Not specialized; specifically (Biol.), not adapted, or set apart, for any particular purpose or function; as, an unspecialized unicellular organism. W. K. Brooks.
Defn: Not performed; not dispatched. [Obs.] Garth.

lg.l: Un*spell", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + spell.]

div.p: Defn: To break the power of (a spell); to release (a person) from the influence of a spell; to disenchant. [R.] Such practices as these, . . . The more judicious Israelites unspelled. Dryden.

lg.l: Un*sphere", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sphere.]

div.p: Defn: To remove, as a planet, from its sphere or orb. Shak.

lg.l: Un*spike", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + spike.]

div.p: Defn: To remove a spike from, as from the vent of a cannon.
Defn: Not spilt or wasted; not shed.

lg.l: Un*spin", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + spin.]

div.p: Defn: To untwist, as something spun.

lg.l: Un*spir"it, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + spirit.]

div.p: Defn: To dispirit. [Obs.] Sir W. Temple.

lg.l: Un*spir"it*al*ize, v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + spiritualize.]

div.p: Defn: To deprive of spiritually. South.

lg.l: Un*spleened", a. Etym: [1st pref. un- + spleen.]

div.p: Defn: Deprived of a spleen.
Defn: Not spotted; free from spot or stain; especially, free from moral stain; unblemished; immaculate; as, an unspotted reputation. — Un*spot"ted*ness, n.

lg.l: Un*squire", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + squire.]

div.p: Defn: To divest of the title or privilege of an esquire. Swift.

lg.l: Defn: Not stable; not firm, fixed, or constant; subject to change or
— Un*sta"ble*ness, n. Chaucer. Unstable equilibrium. See Stable
Un*stack", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + stack.]

div.p: Defn: To remove, or take away, from a stack; to remove, as something constituting a stack.

lg.l: Un*starch", v. t. Etym: [Pref. un- + starch.]

div.p: Defn: To free from starch; to make limp or pliable.

lg.l: Un*state", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + state.]
Defn: To deprive of state or dignity. [R.]
High-battled Cæsar will unstate his happiness. Shak.
Un*steel", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + steel.]

div.p: Defn: To disarm; to soften. Richardson.

lg.l: Un*step", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + step.] (Naut.)

div.p: Defn: To remove, as a mast, from its step.

lg.l: Un*stick", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + stick.]

div.p: Defn: To release, as one thing stuck to another. Richardson.

lg.l: Un*still", a. Etym: [AS. unstille. See Un- not, and Still, a.]

div.p: Defn: Not still; restless. [R.]

lg.l: Un*sting", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + sting.]

div.p: Defn: To disarm of a sting; to remove the sting of. [R.] "Elegant dissertations on virtue and vice . . . will not unsting calamity." J. M. Mason.

lg.l: Un*stitch", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + stitch.]

div.p: Defn: To open by picking out stitches; to take out, or undo, the stitches of; as, to unstitch a seam. Collier.

lg.l: Un*stock", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + stock.]

div.p: 1. To deprive of a stock; to remove the stock from; to loose from that which fixes, or holds fast.
2. To remove from the stocks, as a ship.
1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + stocking.]
Defn: Destitute of stockings. Sir W. Scott.
2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + stocking.]
Defn: Deprived of stockings.

lg.l: Un*stop", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + stop.]

div.p: 1. To take the stopple or stopper from; as, to unstop a bottle or a cask.
2. To free from any obstruction; to open.

lg.l: Un*strain", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + strain.]

div.p: Defn: To relieve from a strain; to relax. B. Jonson.

lg.l: Un*strained", a. Etym: [Pref. un- not + strain.]

div.p: 1. Not strained; not cleared or purified by straining; as, unstrained oil or milk.
2. Not forced; easy; natural; as, a unstrained deduction or inference. Hakewill.
Defn: Not stratified; — applied to massive rocks, as granite, porphyry, etc., and also to deposits of loose material, as the glacial till, which occur in masses without layers or strata.
Defn: Want of strength; weakness; feebleness. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Defn: Nonstriated; unstriped.

lg.l: Un*string", v. t. Etym: [1st pref. un- + string.]

div.p: 1. To deprive of a string or strings; also, to take from a string; as, to unstring beads.
2. To loosen the string or strings of; as, to unstring a harp or a bow.
3. To relax the tension of; to loosen. "His garland they unstring." Dryden.
Defn: Used also figuratively; as, his nerves were unstrung by fear.
1. Not striped.
2. (Nat. Hist.)
Defn: Without marks or striations; nonstriated; as, unstriped muscle fibers.
1. Not studied; not acquired by study; unlabored; natural.
2. Not skilled; unversed; — followed by in.
3. Not spent in study. [Obs.] "To cloak the defects of their unstudied years." Milton.
Defn: Lacking in matter or substance; visionary; chimerical.
